**Solution 3 is the only one with a plausible answer, and I checked its key counterexample.**

**Solutions 1 and 2 are refuted by SQS(8).** Take $H$ to be the Steiner quadruple system on 8 points (the 14 planes of $AG(3,2)$, all 4-edges). Every triple lies in exactly one block, so $\delta_3(H)=1$. Any two planes meet in 0 or 2 points, so each 5-set $F$ contains at most one block, and by counting (14 blocks × 4 five-sets each = 56 = $\binom{8}{5}$) exactly one. Write $F = B \cup \{w\}$. In any cyclic ordering of $F$, the 5 windows are triples; $w$ lies in 3 of them, so the other 2 windows are triples of $B$. Each triple of $B$ lies only in the edge $B$, so those two windows both need $B$, and no system of distinct edges exists. So $H$ has no Berge-$C_5^3$, and the property fails at $n=8$. That forces $n_0 \ge 9$, which rules out both 6 and 7.

**Solution 3's value of 9 is plausible but not fully verified.** The same mechanism cannot block $C_5^3$ at $n=9$. Blocking needs every 5-set to contain a 4-edge whose triples are exclusive to it. Each such block covers $n-4=5$ five-sets, so about 126/5 ≈ 26 blocks would be needed, using about 104 exclusive triples, but $\binom{9}{3}=84$. This counting shows that this particular mechanism fails at $n=9$. I did not rule out every other obstruction for every $t$ at $n \ge 9$, so 9 is the best-supported answer rather than a proof.

CHOICE: 3
